Below, we delineate the reviewer's and editor’s questions, concerns, and requests regarding our original submission, and we detail the ways in which we have addressed each item. All comments have been copied verbatim to avoid misinterpretation.


## Editor

### 1. Please ensure that your manuscript meets PLOS ONE's style requirements, including those for file naming.


### 2. Please note that PLOS One has specific guidelines on code sharing for submissions in which author-generated code underpins the findings in the manuscript. In these cases, we expect all author-generated code to be made available without restrictions upon publication of the work.


### 3. ## Reviewer 1

### 1. The introduction mentions the capability of machine learning models to provide insights into individualized risk factors, leading to tailored momentary supports. Does the present model in the study enable this? Is it possible to generate feature importance rankings for given individuals?



### 2. Related, a justification for not conducting model training within-persons is needed. To deploy these models for interventions, it seems that a “base” model trained on many people is important, but ideally this model can adapt when it is applied to a given individual (i.e., learning from incorrect predictions during the first few weeks).



### 3. Could you provide sensitivity and specificity of the final model? These performance metrics are common in machine learning and easier to interpret than auROC (especially for non-ML audiences). Perhaps prediction labels could be made for discrete 24-hour windows, leading to day-level sensitivity/specificity. Accuracy may also be helpful.


### 4. Does model sensitivity change as an individual drinks more (i.e., sensitivity to detect first lapse versus second, and so forth)? This may have implications regarding within-person training and the reliability of the model overtime as an individual proceeds through recovery.


### 5. Please provide a definition of “feature scoring epoch” when the term is first introduced. (Line 225)


### 6. The cross-validation approach has many facets and jargon. A narrative description of this process may be more digestible, and potentially an accompanying figure.


### 7. How was ‘past alcohol use’ measured? More detail is needed on how this was measured, particularly regarding timing and amount, especially given its feature importance.


### 8. In the abstract, the description around the timing of the prediction is confusing. “predicting next day lapses up to two weeks in advance”. Does this mean prediction of the next day or something that happens in two weeks? Another example is line 105-106: “predicting lapse probability in a 24-hour window that begins two weeks in the future). It is not clear what begins two weeks in the future?


### 9. A definition for early recovery at first mention would be helpful.


### 10. In the discussion, a consideration for how the results may or may not transfer to a sample as those with harm reduction (versus abstinence) goals would improve the implications


### 11. How was compensation prorated for compliance?


### 12. Was other substance use considered as a predictor?


### 13. There is some question regarding the clinical utility of the 2 – week lag, could that be discussed?
